title: Shark Attacks
text:
The Global Shark Attack File (GSAF) is a worldwide historical database maintained by the Shark Research Institute that documents reported shark-human interactions across the globe. Drawing on over a century of cleaned incident records from 1901 through 2018, this project explores where shark encounters happen, what people were doing at the time, and how those encounters typically end.
Pop culture and sensational headlines often paint sharks as relentless predators, fueling widespread fear of entering the ocean. In reality, that fear is far out of proportion to the actual risk: considering the hundreds of millions of ocean visits each year, shark encounters are extraordinarily rare, and roughly four out of five recorded incidents with a known outcome are non-fatal.
Use the navigation bar above to explore the data. The Map page colors countries around the world by their total number of recorded shark attacks, highlighting major coastal hotspots like the United States, Australia, and South Africa. The Trends page breaks down fatal versus non-fatal incidents across the most common water activities—showing how activities like surfing and swimming account for the most encounters while remaining overwhelmingly survivable.
